composition: Nominal composition Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%), referred to as "17Al". The EDS-measured chemistry (Table 1) is Fe 43.2, Mn 34.8, Al 17.0, Cu 5.0 at.%. Iron is the base element; Mn at ~35 at.% is added to promote the precipitation kinetics of the hard β-Mn phase that is mainly responsible for the ultra-high and flexible hardness; Al is the principal density-reducing element (about 0.1 g/cm³ per 1 wt.% Al) and also takes part in the β-Mn and D0₃ precipitation behaviour, while Cu is added to accelerate the aging-hardening response and further raise hardness. The Al variation across the 15Al/17Al/19Al series is achieved by substituting Al for Fe, with Mn (~35 at.%) and Cu (~5 at.%) held essentially constant.
conclusions: This 625 °C/1 h condition illustrates the rapid, high-temperature branch of the 17Al alloy's aging behaviour: a single α (BCC) matrix is essentially fully converted to β-Mn within just 1 h, producing 813.0 ± 20.8 HV and placing the sample on a nearly time-independent hardness plateau of ~813–878 HV over 1–10 h. It is not the peak-hardness state of the 17Al alloy — that peak (924.9 ± 25.8 HV) is reached at 575 °C for 6 h — but it belongs to the ultra-wide, flexible hardness window of 253.4–965.6 HV established across the Fe-35Mn-(15,17,19)Al-5Cu series by simple aging treatments. Compared with the 15Al alloy, the higher-Al 17Al (and 19Al) alloys transform more slowly, require higher optimal aging temperatures (550–600 °C for 17Al vs 525–600 °C for 15Al) and reach slightly lower peak hardness. The work demonstrates a route to "one material, multiple uses": parts can be shaped in the soft solution-treated state and then aged to a chosen hardness, cutting the cost and difficulty of producing hard, wear-resistant components. The remaining limitation is toughness, which decreases with increasing Al content (K_IC of the hardest states: 8.6 MPa·m^1/2 for 15Al, 6.6 MPa·m^1/2 for 17Al, 3.5 MPa·m^1/2 for 19Al), so an optimal hardness–toughness balance warrants further study.
mechanisms: Aging at 625 °C for 1 h drives an almost complete α (BCC) → β-Mn phase transformation in the 17Al alloy; because β-Mn has a very high intrinsic hardness (over 10 GPa), the increasing volume fraction of β-Mn is the dominant source of the ultra-high hardness (813.0 ± 20.8 HV vs a 259.8 ± 1.5 HV solution-treated baseline).

β-Mn is a Mn-rich phase, so its nucleation and growth require the rejection of Fe, Al and Cu into the surrounding matrix; the expelled Al stabilizes a new BCC phase and the expelled Cu, whose solubility in Fe-based alloys is limited, forms the FCC Cu-rich phase at the β-Mn interfaces. This yields the sequence α → α + FCC Cu-rich → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC → β-Mn + BCC + FCC Cu-rich.

Raising the aging temperature accelerates the precipitation and growth of β-Mn (both governed by atomic diffusion) because of a greater driving force and faster atomic diffusion; consequently the α→β-Mn transformation of the 17Al alloy is complete after only 1 h at 600 °C and above, but needs ~6 h at 550 °C and is still incomplete after 10 h at 525 °C — explaining the nearly time-independent hardness plateau at 625 °C.

Increasing the Al content slows the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn, because (i) the extra Al enriches around the growing Mn-rich β-Mn and hinders its further precipitation and growth, and (ii) higher Al promotes the formation of a larger amount of the Al-rich, Al-stabilized D0₃ phase whose depletion is a prerequisite for β-Mn nucleation and growth.

Increasing the Al content slightly enhances the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn through solid-solution strengthening (Al dissolved in β-Mn rises from 14.3 at.% in 15Al to 16.3 at.% in 17Al to 17.5 at.% in 19Al), but at the same time increases the volume fraction of the softer BCC and FCC Cu-rich phases at the β-Mn interfaces, lowering the absolute volume fraction of β-Mn and hence the overall hardness; the FCC Cu-rich phase also helps toughness because it is more ductile, so its decrease with increasing Al content degrades K_IC.
microstructure: The parent solution-treated state of the 17Al alloy is a single α (BCC) phase (confirmed by EBSD, Fig. 3). After aging at 625 °C for 1 h, the α (BCC) matrix had almost completely transformed into β-Mn, and numerous fine precipitates, identified by EBSD as BCC and FCC Cu-rich phases, were distributed within the β-Mn. SE-SEM of this condition (Fig. 8) shows a uniform matrix with fine "New precipitates" resolved only in the magnified inset. The associated phase interfaces are β-Mn/FCC Cu-rich and β-Mn/BCC. The microstructural sequence proposed for these Fe-Mn-Al-Cu alloys during aging is α (BCC) matrix → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase, with the α→β-Mn transformation essentially complete for the 17Al alloy at 625 °C/1 h. For the 17Al alloy generally, β-Mn first forms along α grain boundaries with small short rod-shaped particles inside the grains, and higher aging temperatures (600 °C and above) complete the transformation within only 1 h. Note that the direct TEM/EDS interface work (Fig. 12) and nanoindentation (Fig. 13) of the 17Al alloy were performed on the 575 °C/6 h peak-hardness sample, and its XRD trace (Fig. 10) was measured at 575 °C/1 h, not on this 625 °C/1 h condition.
processing: The alloy was produced by vacuum induction melting of high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials under an argon atmosphere. The ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, then hot-rolled into plates 4 mm thick, from which 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ specimens were cut by electrical discharge machining for hardness testing and microstructure characterization. The parent state of this sample was obtained by solution treatment at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching, which leaves a single α (BCC) phase. The specific sample described here was then aged at 625 °C for 1 h and water quenched. Aging of this alloy was explored over 525–650 °C for 1, 3, 6 and 10 h, so this 625 °C/1 h condition lies at the short-time end of the high-temperature aging regime.
properties: Vickers hardness of this sample (room temperature, HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester, 9.8 N load for 15 s, average of 5 measurements) is 813.0 ± 20.8 HV, measured on an electrolytically polished 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ specimen. The common solution-treated baseline of the 17Al alloy is 259.8 ± 1.5 HV, so the 625 °C/1 h aging raises hardness by a factor of about three. Compared with the other 625 °C aging times of the 17Al alloy, this sample sits on a nearly time-independent hardness plateau of ~813–878 HV between 1 and 10 h (872.0 ± 24.4 HV at 3 h, 878.4 ± 28.3 HV at 6 h, 870.5 ± 24.9 HV at 10 h). Characterization techniques applied here were Vickers hardness testing (HVS-1000) and secondary-electron SEM (ZEISS Sigma 300 operated at 5 kV); samples were prepared by electrolytic polishing in a 10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol mixture. No tensile, fracture-toughness, physical or chemical property data are reported specifically for this 625 °C/1 h condition.
summary: The 17Al sample is the Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%) low-density steel (17 at.% Al nominal) in the state produced by aging the solution-treated alloy at 625 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching. It belongs to a series of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels designed to achieve ultra-high, widely tunable hardness through the rapid precipitation of the ultra-hard β-Mn phase; this particular condition is one point of the aging-hardening map of the 17Al alloy and gives a Vickers hardness of 813.0 ± 20.8 HV. The paper's central question is how the Al content (15, 17, 19 at.%) controls the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn and thereby the achievable hardening.
unmapped: The parent solution-treated 17Al alloy has a Vickers hardness of 259.8 ± 1.5 HV, which is the common baseline for all 17Al aging conditions including this 625 °C/1 h sample.

The 17Al alloy aged at 625 °C shows a nearly time-independent hardness plateau of ~813–878 HV across 1–10 h (813.0 ± 20.8 HV at 1 h, 872.0 ± 24.4 HV at 3 h, 878.4 ± 28.3 HV at 6 h, 870.5 ± 24.9 HV at 10 h); the peak hardness of the 17Al alloy (924.9 ± 25.8 HV) is instead reached at 575 °C for 6 h, so this 625 °C/1 h sample is not the peak-hardness state.
